newsitem.title: UK: Scientists link leukaemia to French nuclear plant.
newsitem.headline: Scientists link leukaemia to French nuclear plant.

text.p: French scientists said on Friday that children who played regularly on a beach near a nuclear reprocessing plant were three times more likely to get leukaemia.
Eating local fish and shellfish at least once a week also increased the risk, researchers told the British Medical Journal.
The research by French government scientists Jean-Francois Viel and Dominique Pobel was based on 27 cases of leukaemia in people aged under 25 around La Hague plant in Normandy.

The state-owned nuclear materials group Cogema (Compagnie generale des matieres nucleaires), which runs the Hague plant, said the scientists' survey was carried out on such small samples of population that its conclusions were baseless.
Cogema said its own numerous and regular surveys of the plant's environmental impact showed radiation to be less than one percent of natural radioactivity.

The French scientists told the British Medical Journal: "There is some convincing evidence in childhood leukaemia of a causal role for environmental radiation exposure from recreational activity on beaches.
"New methods for identifying the environmental pathways, focusing on marine ecosystems are warranted," they added.
But the researchers said there was no link between either the mothers' or the fathers' occupational exposure to radiation. "Our data clearly do not support a genuine association," the said.

Following public concern about possible leukaemia clusters, they called for more research to be carried out around La Hague as well as the Sellafield and Dounreay nuclear reprocessing plants in Britain.
The researchers found that children who visited beaches near La Hague at least once a month were three times more likely to develop leukaemia.
They studied two groups from 1978 through to 1993 --- 27 cases of leukaemia and 192 who were healthy and unaffected.
